author: Saatvik Singh
title: A conversation with Prof. (Dr.) Raghav Sharma  on what sustainable peace means in the context of Afghanistan?
content:
A conversation with Prof. (Dr.) Raghav Sharma  

Dr. Raghav Sharma is Professor and Director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at O.P. Jindal Global University, India. He is the author of Nation, Ethnicity and the Conflict in Afghanistan: Political Islam and the Rise of Ethno–Politics (1992–1996). He has worked in Afghanistan’s humanitarian sector, taught at the University of Erfurt, Germany, and consulted for organisations including the Aga Khan Development Network and Integrity Watch Afghanistan. He writes on Afghanistan and his current research examines relations between the Afghan Taliban and Pakistan.

 

What does sustainable peace mean in the context of Afghanistan, beyond the contours of armed conflict?

 

Sustainable Peace in the Afghan context is not just the absence of violence. What we have seen over the last five years is what literature would refer to as the idea of negative peace. There is the absence of physical violence, but other forms of structural violence persist in the country through various forms of inequality that are being perpetuated under the current regime in Afghanistan. So sustainable peace would be a peace where you know the Afghans would be able to come to terms with the difficult past of the last four and a half decades. It would entail creating a society that is, I would not say equal, but equitable. 

It would be socially more inclusive and can make the very difficult political and social adjustments of grappling with what is a deeply heterogeneous society. We do not see that happening at the moment and it is unlikely to happen under the current dispensation. So sustainable peace essentially would entail political, economic and social reconfiguration that comes to terms with the deeply heterogeneous society that Afghanistan is, while also addressing the inequalities and structural violence that persist under the current regime. On neither of those counts do we see any positive movement forward.

 

What are the most promising pathways to building sustainable peace in Afghanistan today?

 

Today the pathway to sustainable peace seems very dim, and that is because any pathway that proposes any alternative to the ruling dispensation is not being taken too kindly. Building sustainable peace would involve not just government actors, but it would also involve mobilising people from civil society, people at the grassroots level and mobilising independent voices. The space for that has not only shrunk, it has almost become non-existent. Voices that were articulating their vision of what peace should look like have been silenced in more ways than one, and they have very few allies outside the country to support their vision. I also think that the country is not politically ready to work towards sustainable peace, which is not actually an easy path to tread down on.

Right now, there is peace in the sense that there is no armed conflict, and that is because the perpetrators of violence are today in power. However, the challenge in Afghanistan is that regime change has been so frequent that the line between the victim and the perpetrator has been blurred. Someone who was a perpetrator under one regime became a victim under the next and vice versa. Building sustainable peace would inevitably pose political challenges for whoever is in power, whether this is the Taliban or tomorrow it is some other dispensation in power, because this would entail having difficult conversations. We saw an effort being made towards this end when there was a commission that was set up under the Republic to investigate war crimes that were committed during the period of Civil War, but also during the period of communist rule. That report indicted many people in power within the republic at that time. It called for taking measures to build peace that would not have sat very well with those in power, and those efforts were snuffed out.

What we are dealing with today is a totalitarian entity that has a very different vision of what state and society should look like. They operate in a very puritanical religious framework, in which there is very little to no space for alternative visions of any kind. So, I do not see sustainable peace finding fertile ground in the current context. One very good example that comes to mind essentially is, for example, the excellent work that Matiullah Wesa (Afghan activist) was doing on education. It was something non-political, because he was not telling anyone to change their policies. He just harped on the idea of why education is important and the need to take education to every corner of the country as a tool for social change. This got him jailed. Unfortunately, we hardly saw anybody speak up for him from the international community. Afghans unfortunately lack international allies who would speak for them. It is important to keep this in mind in the context of our discussion. 

Afghanistan is now a forgotten story. It has receded to the background. There are larger conflicts that have captured the international attention of international audiences, amidst a systematic breakdown of the rules-based order. A lot of established rules have been challenged. What was the fringe has now, in a sense, been mainstream. The Taliban was unpalatable. They were medieval. Today they are slowly being politically mainstreamed by engaging in trade with other countries. Given these circumstances, I think the possibility of any meaningful work for sustainable peace seems very unlikely.

 

How does social inequality and the exclusion of women and minority communities affect the prospects for lasting peace in Afghanistan?

 

It affects lasting peace because while you may have stability at the macro-level and the absence of violence, it does not mean the minorities repose faith in the system. There is growing discontent under the surface. Many are frustrated that they are politically excluded and socially marginalised, and see no viable economic prospects, which are a route to social mobility for these communities. Many would be waiting for the right opportunity to challenge the status quo. The problem is that they lack a viable, credible leadership that could channelise their grievances. It creates a situation of latent conflict that can always be exploited by an external power. Afghanistan has a long history of that, where a disarticulation between the ruling dispensation and the society it rules over has been instrumentalised by external powers.

We have seen thousands of Hazaras forced off land in provinces like Daikundi. The Taliban cabinet is entirely a Pashtun cabinet, with no political representation outside the Taliban. It is more of a victor's cabinet than in 1996. In 1996 the Taliban's first cabinet included two non-Taliban members, one of them a woman, which is not the case today. That exclusion is not just ethnic but ideological. It only includes Pashtuns ideologically aligned with the Taliban, not non-Pashtun commanders within the ranks. In the early days there were revolts within the Taliban's ranks by non-Pashtuns like Maulvi Mehdi. Similarly, Tajik and Uzbek commanders staged revolts that were snuffed out, resulting in those commanders being tossed into prison. This exclusion is still brewing under the surface. On 17th July, 2026 for the first time in five years, a district in Badakhshan fell for a couple of hours to a new opposition group, the Homeland soldiers, who captured the district centre, raised their own flag, and made the Taliban surrender. There have also been multiple instances of local commanders targeting Chinese mining officials in Badakhshan.

So, this political, social and economic exclusion is brewing under the surface, and could eventually challenge the stable but negative peace we have, because it will open up channels for these grievances to be instrumentalised by external players, who will wait for the right opportunity. The economy has not collapsed, but it is not doing great either, and in the long run people who feel they have no stake and no economic future would be willing to take up arms for a paltry sum. Afghans who were welcomed by Pakistan and Iran before now see their neighbours facing situations of war. The population of Afghanistan is much higher than in the 90s, much younger and far more aspirational in terms of what the state should deliver.

 

Based on your experience, what role can local communities and traditional institutions play in conflict prevention and peacebuilding?

 

Earlier it was mostly the village elders, village based shuras and tribal institutions that played an important role in diffusing conflict and shaping outcomes at the local level. Now due to armed conflict, the existing socio-political contracts have changed, shifting the power balance from the traditional tribal chiefs and village heads to armed commanders who wield the gun. The ability of these traditional structures to shape peace outcomes has not been eliminated, but it has been diminished significantly. The mullahs carried little weight in traditional Afghan society. Their role was usually nonpolitical and limited to ceremonial occasions like birth, death, circumcision and marriage, the weighty political role was reserved for the tribal malik. That has changed, because you now have many armed commanders who wield power by the gun. It reflects how religion has acquired greater salience, and the fact that many of these commanders come from communities once socially and politically marginalised. So, the shuras and jirgas (collective councils) remain important but are not the only conduits. Any initiative to build peace would also have to take on board religious figures, who wield far more clout and social and cultural capital than forty years ago. It would entail working with many genders. Though how much power they can wield under the current dispensation remains questionable. In areas like Bamiyan and the Panjshir Valley, you have people known as the safedrish, or White Beards, respected for both their age and their wisdom. Many informal mechanisms for peace building in central Afghanistan take on board these old men, even though they hold no institutional position.

The real challenge is how you involve women, because that is one section disproportionately impacted by conflict yet without a voice. One window into their world is local folklore. Afghan women in the south-southeast take recourse to composing couplets known as the landay, which very often make powerful political and social commentaries on the prevailing state of affairs. There are underground networks that work with women's voices. So, this would entail working officially with the existing tribal councils and religious leaders, but also with grassroots actors who operate under the radar. Any work to this end is not going to be a swift institutionalised process, due to various factors at play.

 

Afghanistan currently has a lack of strong state institutions. Can peace exist without legitimate institutions that represent the citizens?

 

This is a loaded and difficult question. How do you gauge the legitimacy of the system? Is it only through elections? If so, even the last Republican regime was deeply illegitimate, because participation was at an all time low and corruption and nepotism were rife. This is an uncomfortable fact. During the Republic, many people were turning to Taliban institutions, particularly the judiciary. The Taliban had set up their own mobile courts to resolve disputes. The people turned to them despite the Taliban's brutal methods because they were considered efficient, non-corrupt, and delivered swift justice, unlike the courts of the Republic, which were inefficient and blatantly corrupt, and over time lost their legitimacy.

Legitimacy is very contextual, it depends on who you speak to and where you are and may not always accrue from institutions being democratic in the conventional sense. Are they seen as democratic and validated by the people? Certainly the current regime projects power far more strongly than the Republic ever did. After the fall of the monarchy, this is perhaps one regime that has managed to get the entire country under its administrative control. It extracts revenue far more efficiently and has plugged pilferage on border customs, an important source of revenue. There is also an interesting study from the beginning of this year on how more women are claiming property rights under the Taliban's courts than under the Republic, for a multitude of reasons.

It is not a black and white picture. Some institutions like the judiciary had become deeply corrupt under the Republic, and many people have more faith in certain Taliban institutions than they had under the Republic. That, however, does not mean that the Taliban's political institutions enjoy the same legitimacy, or that Afghans who lost faith in the Republic wanted the Taliban. The fact remains that the current system has snuffed out dissent, that you have human rights violations, a lot documented, but many undocumented. A lot of dissent is crushed out by censorship before it is even expressed. In a closed system without elections, human rights violations, media closures, and illegal detentions can serve as indicators of the regime's legitimacy. 

 

Is it fair to then say that even though controversial, the current regime may still be legitimate in some ways?

 

Many Afghans do not agree with it. I will give you one example from a different period. Najibullah, who ruled up till 1992, was considered illegitimate and a stooge of the Russians, but also a shrewd and cunning politician. When his government fell and the Mujahideen came to power, everybody thought we finally have sovereignty back and things are going to be right. However , there was so much violence and chaos over the civil war that graffiti popped up across Kabul saying, "take back your seven donkeys", referring to the seven Mujahideen parties in Peshawar, "and give us back our ox", referring to Najib. After he was killed, and during my countrywide visits, I recall seeing huge public rallies organised for Najib, his posters and postcards everywhere. He had rightly predicted, long before he fell, that you would see bloodshed in every street and that Pakistan would have a huge role in Afghanistan if not stopped. He was reinvented as the great nationalist leader and not remembered as the communist. So, legitimacy is very contextual and evaluative, and it changes with time.

 

How do the Taliban’s current education policies reflect their vision for Afghanistan, and what implications do these policies have for the country’s long term prospects for peace?

 

I do not think the current education policies of the Taliban augur well for the future of the country or for building sustainable peace. Ever since they came to power, they have made sweeping changes to the curriculum. To be fair, they are not the only ones that have done this. Every regime since the 1970s has sought to capture the education curriculum for its political ends, because mass public education is the best way to shape and indoctrinate young minds.

What we have seen is a whittling down of secular education. The Ministers of Education and Higher Education have claimed that secular education is basically ‘useless’ and religious education has meaning. Subjects like civic education have been done away with, and not just Islamic education but the teachings of Amir al-Mu'minin, the leader of the Taliban, have also been introduced. A certain kind of religious teaching, an interpretation of Islam that sits well with the Taliban's, is being enforced. A lot of what the Taliban practise and profess is at odds with how Islam has been practised in the Afghan context. So Islamic subjects have gone up, while science and mathematics have been given diminished value. In the long run this creates a huge challenge, because it is not just that girls are not getting education, but even boys, and the kind of education they are getting is undergoing a fundamental qualitative shift. A lot of them are going to madrasas, and not all madrasas give an education open to knowledge or tolerant of heterogeneity. So this is going to change the social fabric in pronounced ways, and the worldview of the young generation coming out of Afghan schools. People in charge of these institutions do not necessarily possess the requisite qualifications, they are in charge because of their ideological affinity.

This is going to be a challenge for Afghanistan and the region, because these people will have a worldview that does not sit well with the rest of the world. Moreover, young Afghans today lack 21st century skills. Right now the countries offering scholarships are getting Afghans educated under the Republic's system. That will change dramatically over the next ten years, producing a very different bunch of kids imbibing a different worldview, generating skepticism about whether it is safe to have them over. The flip side is that education can be the biggest harbinger of social change. Exposing these kids to a worldview and skill set outside of what they know can bring positive change. Education would also give them the skill set to critique and question, which is not something they are currently interested in. So the current education system is going to inculcate a narrow worldview, not accommodative of social heterogeneity, that may even normalise, in certain situations, the use of violence for political and ideological ends. That will be a challenge in the long run, leading to social friction the country may not be equipped to handle.
